In just seven days in November, some of the world’s most critical technology services experienced significant disruptions. Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Workday, and others made headlines for failures that interrupted business operations and everyday life.


The timing fueled speculation about coordinated cyberattacks and AI-driven sabotage.


The reality is considerably less exciting and far more useful.


These were ordinary failures inside extraordinarily complex systems. And while the outages were spectacular, much of the work that prevents the next one is not.


Resilience is built through the decidedly unglamorous work of simplifying technology, understanding what’s happening inside it, continuously experimenting with how it fails, and learning from what happens next.

## Complexity Becomes A Failure Domain


Digital progress creates complexity. Organizations add applications, integrations, cloud services, automation, data platforms, and now AI. Each delivers new capability, but it can also add another dependency and another path for failure to travel.


Let that sink in.


Telling technology leaders to “simplify” that environment is easy — doing it can feel nearly impossible. Most organizations didn’t deliberately design the complexity they have today. It accumulated over years of modernization, acquisitions, urgent business demands, regulatory requirements, and perfectly reasonable technology decisions. Pull on one thread, and you quickly discover three other systems, a critical business process, and a team that depends on it. But i


s there hope?


Y


e


s


.


- **T-Mobile** consolidated eight commerce systems plagued by fragile integrations, manual deployments, and launch-day incidents. Its cloud-native replacement uses active-active multiregion operations, automation, and infrastructure as code and has handled 10x traffic spikes without performance degradation.


- [Slack](https://slack.engineering/slacks-migration-to-a-cellular-architecture/?mode=reply) responded to a 2021 cloud-network incident by spending 18 months migrating critical services from a monolithic to cellular architecture, limiting how far failures can spread.


- **The Hong Kong Jockey Club** mapped more than 17,000 nodes across 500 systems to uncover dependencies that had become difficult to see.


- **Wendy’s** dedicates significant product development capacity to technical debt and platform stability rather than layering new functionality onto fragile foundations.


- [TIAA](https://www.cio.com/article/4210980/wide-ranging-transformation-at-tiaa-enables-dozens-of-business-use-cases.html) started with more than 80% of workloads on fragmented, end-of-life platforms. Its multiyear modernization has since cut technical debt nearly in half while consolidating middleware, data platforms, and decades-old processes.

That’s modernization doing more than adding capability.


Reducing unnecessary complexity reduces the places where failure can hide and the distance it can travel.


## Start Making Your Systems More Resilient


You won’t simplify decades of accumulated complexity overnight. But you don’t have to wait for a sweeping modernization program to make progress. Start with three things:


1. **See what can fail together.** Invest in observability that reveals dependencies and connects technical signals to business outcomes. Don’t just ask whether individual components are up. Understand which critical services depend on them and how far a failure could travel.


2. **Break things before they break themselves.** Test more than failover on paper. Take components down, simulate degraded dependencies, test rollback, and practice recovery under realistic conditions. The goal isn’t to predict every failure but to learn how your systems actually behave when assumptions prove wrong.


3. **Learn, adapt, repeat.** Treat incidents and near misses as opportunities to make the system stronger, not to find someone to blame. Give engineers room to surface weaknesses, experiment with solutions, and change the plan when reality doesn’t match the runbook.


This is the decidedly unglamorous work of resilience: retiring an integration, instrumenting an opaque service, testing recovery again, and fixing the weakness that almost caused an outage.


Resilience isn’t something organizations discover during an outage — it’s the product of thousands of mundane decisions that they make before one occurs.


Our new report,


[The Tragically Mundane Story Of Tech Outages: Fragile Technology Foundations Undermine An AI Future](https://www.forrester.com/go?objectid=res206014) , explores what November’s extraordinary string of ordinary failures reveals about technology resilience and what executives should do next.
